name: Antimilitarism
summary: Antimilitarism opposes militarism: large standing armies kept in aggressive readiness, the political power of the military, and arms build-ups that divert resources from civilian needs. Unlike pacifism it does not reject all war or defence, and it spans socialists, civil libertarians, constitutional conservatives and Japanese post-war pacifist constitutionalism.
scope: A broad family profile based on the Second International socialist tradition (Karl Liebknecht, Militarism and Anti-Militarism, 1907), Eisenhower's warning on the military-industrial complex, the Thoreau and Founders' tradition of opposing standing armies, and Japan's Article 9. It excludes absolute pacifism and strict non-resistance. Most statements outside war, armies and foreign policy are unaddressed, so those answers are inferred and low confidence.

keyFigures.name: Karl Liebknecht
keyFigures.role: German socialist whose 1907 book on militarism and anti-militarism set out the Social-Democratic case.

keyFigures.name: Dwight D. Eisenhower
keyFigures.role: US president whose 1961 farewell address warned against the military-industrial complex.

keyFigures.name: Henry David Thoreau
keyFigures.role: American writer whose tax refusal over the Mexican-American War is cited as a libertarian-civic antimilitarist example.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Antimilitarists frame military budgets as diverting money from health and education, so they lean toward public healthcare, though the creed itself does not address it.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Not a core issue; the socialist and civic strands tend to favour it, but antimilitarism as such is silent on wages.

public-ownership.rationale: Socialist antimilitarists favour it while constitutionalist and civic strands do not; the position is not defined by the ideology.

unions-good.rationale: Liebknecht's socialist antimilitarism was bound up with labour organisation and youth leagues, but unions are not a defining issue.

property-fundamental.rationale: Libertarian and constitutionalist antimilitarists favour strong property rights while socialists do not; the strands split.

cut-welfare.rationale: Antimilitarists argue spending should shift from arms to social needs, so cutting welfare to fund arms runs against their priorities.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: No relation to the core issue; strands split between civil libertarians and progressives.

strong-leader.rationale: Antimilitarists oppose concentrated war-making power and stress civilian and popular control over military decisions (Cockburn's opposition to military rule).

state-harmful.rationale: Libertarian antimilitarists like Thoreau lean this way but socialist and constitutional strands accept the state.

limit-guns.rationale: The right-wing strand favours an armed citizen militia, which pulls against gun limits; strands diverge, tilted slightly against.

empower-police-military.rationale: Antimilitarism is defined as opposing a large military and its civil power; Eisenhower and Liebknecht both warn against strengthening it. The sources set out the underlying principle but do not state a position on this specific statement.

more-religion-public.rationale: Unrelated; religious and secular antimilitarists both exist.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Unrelated to the core; strands split.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Cockburn's feminist antimilitarism leans yes, but the right-wing strand differs.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Constitutionalist antimilitarists may value national tradition while socialists are internationalist.

gradual-change.rationale: Strands split between reformist constitutionalists and radical socialists and civil disobedients.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Socialist and pacifist strands favour international bodies; constitutionalists oppose foreign entanglements.

free-trade.rationale: Strands split; the socialist strand is sceptical, the constitutionalist one accepts trade without entanglements.

nation-first.rationale: The socialist strand is internationalist, and the Second International held wars to be national bourgeois rivalry.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): the old wording asked whether military intervention abroad is sometimes necessary to protect human rights, and this disagreement rested on opposing particular interventions or interventions by particular powers, which doesn't say it is never necessary.

reviewHistory.rationale: Antimilitarism opposes aggressive readiness for war and foreign military adventures, though it does not reject all war.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

revolution-justified.rationale: Liebknecht links militarism's end to the end of capitalism, but the civic and constitutional strands reject revolution.

experts-over-public.rationale: Eisenhower urged an alert citizenry to check the defence establishment, and the ideology stresses popular control of war and peace.

central-planning.rationale: Socialist antimilitarists may agree; others do not.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Central banking is not an antimilitarist concern, and the strands that make up the ideology hold opposite views on money.

one-party-rule.rationale: Antimilitarists reject military rule and concentrated coercive power, and the ideology stresses civil authority over the military. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

democracy-best.rationale: The Second International's antimilitarism claimed that standing armies negate democracy and wanted the people to decide on war and peace.

workers-councils.rationale: Only the socialist strand would assent.

political-violence-never.rationale: Miller's definition says antimilitarism does not reject war in all cases, and Liebknecht distinguished wars; adherents are split between pacifists and those who accept some violence.

war-builds-character.rationale: Antimilitarists cite war's harm to civilians and its costs; militarist glorification of war is exactly what they oppose.

separate-church-state.rationale: The sources do not link militarism to church-state relations, and both secular and religious antimilitarists exist.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Eisenhower and Liebknecht both treat private profit in arms and armed force as a danger; privatised defence is opposed.

military-superiority.rationale: Antimilitarism opposes maintaining large forces in aggressive readiness; Eisenhower called each weapon a theft from the hungry.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Socialist antimilitarists agree; civic and constitutional strands do not.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Equality of outcomes is not an antimilitarist question; socialist adherents may favour it while libertarians reject it.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Libertarian antimilitarists lean yes, socialists no.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Antimilitarists oppose compulsory duties such as service; Thoreau placed conscience above state demands.

limit-population.rationale: Population policy is not an antimilitarist topic; neither the socialist nor constitutionalist strands take a common line.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The sources object to militarised industry rather than to industrial civilization as a whole, so the claim is not endorsed.

direct-action.rationale: Liebknecht treats individual refusal as the anarchist method and favours mass movement and parliament; Thoreau's civil disobedience is a direct-action tradition, so the strands split.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Abolishing the division of labor is a utopian-socialist theme not found in the antimilitarist sources.

production-for-use.rationale: Liebknecht ties militarism to capitalist profit, so the socialist strand favours production for use; others silent.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Liebknecht cites Paris 1899 as treating war as a consequence of capitalism and tying militarism to it, though adherents outside the socialist strand disagree. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

taxation-theft.rationale: Thoreau refused tax over war, but most strands accept taxation; split.

conscription.rationale: Draft resisters and Liebknecht oppose the conscript army of militarism, but Liebknecht's alternative is a universal citizen militia and Second International majorities did not reject compulsory service as such.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Antimilitarism seeks to prevent international war and opposes aggressive military readiness; expansion by force is the opposite.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Diaspora return rights are not covered by the sources, and antimilitarists hold varied views.

force-without-un.rationale: The ideology opposes aggressive readiness and foreign adventures and is wary of unilateral force.

class-collaboration.rationale: Liebknecht saw the army as used against strikers; the socialist strand favours class struggle, while others are silent.

workers-nation.rationale: The Second International held that workers should not take part in wars between national bourgeoisies and favoured international brotherhood.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Cockburn's feminist antimilitarism criticises militarised gender roles.

ban-interest.rationale: Banning interest is not an antimilitarist topic.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Liebknecht treats the army as a tool of ruling-class domination at home, but other strands do not generalise to the state. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

national-mission.rationale: Spreading a form of government by force is aggressive military readiness, which the ideology opposes.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Eisenhower warned of misplaced power in the defence-industry complex, but a general charge against elites is not a tenet.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Defence is the one function the night-watchman state keeps, which antimilitarists limit; constitutionalists may accept it.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Religious conversion law is not an antimilitarist topic.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Antimilitarism opposes arming against hostile states, though the socialist case is debated.

population-transfer.rationale: Expelling minorities rests on coercive force and civilian harm which antimilitarists reject. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Miller's definition aims at preventing international war and the ideology opposes aggression, though not all force is rejected.

separated-powers.rationale: Cockburn and constitutionalists oppose military rule and stress checks on the army; the Founders' standing-army fears rest on divided power.

vanguard-party.rationale: Liebknecht stressed mass movement and education of youth rather than a vanguard.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Eisenhower said arms spending takes from the hungry and the ideology wants resources redirected to needs.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Liebknecht saw the army used against strikers; restrictions on strikes are opposed by the socialist strand.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Agamben's critique of the state of exception, cited in the article, opposes indefinite suspension of law.

party-commands-army.rationale: The ideology wants to curb military political power; party command of the army is partisan control, which is opposed.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Socialist strand yes; constitutionalist strand wary of entanglements.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Concentrated command by one person conflicts with legislative and popular control of war that the ideology favours.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Church governance is not an antimilitarist issue.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Liebknecht and the Second International opposed workers supporting wars between national bourgeoisies; the text does not directly address defeat of one's own government, and non-socialist strands disagree. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: The constitutionalist strand opposes foreign entanglements and standing alliances, but socialists are mostly silent. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

people-in-arms.rationale: Liebknecht and the Second International demanded replacing standing armies with citizen militias, and constitutionalist antimilitarists favour citizen militias.

death-penalty.rationale: The ideology's preference for non-lethal solutions and Thoreau-style conscience lean against it.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Sex education is not an antimilitarist subject.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Teaching creationism is not an antimilitarist question.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Foreign debt is not an antimilitarist topic.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: The article cites Japan's non-nuclear principles as evidence of antimilitarism and the ideology opposes arms build-up. The sources set out the underlying principle but do not state a position on this specific statement.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Antimilitarism seeks peace; this stance risks war, so it leans against.

collective-defense.rationale: The constitutionalist strand opposes entangling alliances and the Japanese model renounces war potential, though some strands accept collective defence.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Church-state power balance is not an antimilitarist subject.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: The ideology opposes domestic uses of the military against the population (militarism at home, Paris 1899).

sacred-ruler.rationale: Sacred rulers and leader cults belong to militarised states; republican strands oppose. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Agamben's critique and Paris 1899 on democratic republicanism oppose rulers above law.

leader-cult.rationale: Cults of leaders accompany militarism, which is the target of the ideology. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

equal-parenting.rationale: Custody presumptions are unrelated to antimilitarism.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Territorial claims based on co-ethnics are a typical cause of war. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

common-currency.rationale: Monetary union is not an antimilitarist question.

no-bailouts.rationale: Bailouts are not an antimilitarist subject.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Liebknecht rejects military strikes and heroic minority acts, preferring organised mass movement.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The socialist strand opposes imperialism (Lenin, Luxemburg), as cited by the article.

patriotic-education.rationale: Liebknecht stresses antimilitarist education of youth against military drilling and indoctrination.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Racial preferences are not an antimilitarist topic.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Socialist strand denies it; other strands silent.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Imperial aspirations are aggressive and opposed. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Constitutionalist strand and Article 9 show entrenched limits on government.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Antimilitarism is an organised political movement.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Territorial revanchism is a standard cause of war that the ideology opposes. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Cockburn's definition of antimilitarism opposes military rule, and its aim is reducing the civil power of the military.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Divorce law is unrelated to antimilitarism.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: London 1896 and Liebknecht refused military credits, which presupposes parliament's control of military budgets.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Arming proxies is aggressive military activity; the ideology opposes it.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Military intervention in another state is the sort of aggression the ideology opposes.

corporate-influence.rationale: Eisenhower's warning about the military-industrial complex is a case of corporate influence on government.

democratic-peace.rationale: The article says antimilitarists regard capitalism and arms interests as drivers of war and are wary of crusades to spread democracy; split.

non-intervention.rationale: The ideology opposes foreign military entanglement, though the statement says for any reason and not all adherents go so far.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Eisenhower called for an alert and knowledgeable citizenry, which requires access to information.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Language purism is not an antimilitarist topic.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The ideology opposes military and coercive rule over civilians. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Lenin and Luxemburg's critiques of imperialism are cited as strands.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Armed removal of rulers is militarised violence the ideology opposes. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

participatory-democracy.rationale: The ideology wants popular rather than military or elite control of war and peace.

assisted-dying.rationale: Assisted dying is not an antimilitarist topic.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: The article shows antimilitarism spanning left and right, which is neutral on the claim.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Employment dispute law is unrelated to antimilitarism.

open-government-data.rationale: Eisenhower urged an informed citizenry to oversee the defence establishment.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Antimilitarists oppose the military as such, so assessing access to it is not a principled issue.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Liebknecht's work centres on resisting military training and drill of youth through antimilitarist youth leagues, a reaction to exactly this.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: The article cites Japan's non-nuclear principles as evidence of antimilitarism.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Opposing foreign entanglements and standing armies supports closing foreign bases, though adherents like Japan's accept alliance bases.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: The article stresses antimilitarists reject military readiness rather than all violence, unlike absolute pacifists.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Glorifying fallen soldiers is part of militarist culture that antimilitarism opposes.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Antimilitarism accepts defensive war but opposes aggressive readiness, and Article 9 renounces war as a means of settling disputes.

municipal-property.rationale: The socialist strand might favour collective ownership and the libertarian strand would not, so adherents are split.

racial-pride.rationale: Antimilitarists do not address racial pride and the strands differ.

free-public-college.rationale: Not a core issue; the socialist and civic strands favour spending on education over arms, as Eisenhower's address contrasts schools with weapons.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Environmental taxation is outside antimilitarism, and adherents divide by wider politics.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its value rests on women's distinct roles, giving their values more weight, a claim about innate nature or no stated position, and the statement now asks only whether women tend to be more compassionate than men.

reviewHistory.rationale: Some antimilitarists link nonviolence to women's perspective, but the creed is not committed either way and adherents split.

arms-reduction.rationale: Eisenhower's address calls for disarmament and warns against arms build-ups, and antimilitarism is defined by opposition to excessive armaments.

capital-controls.rationale: Capital controls are outside antimilitarism, and adherents divide by wider politics.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Socialist antimilitarists in the Liebknecht line wanted the state transformed, but liberal and conservative strands do not, so it is a mild inference.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Antimilitarism is silent on religion and spans secular socialists, Christian pacifists and constitutionalists, so adherents are split.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Japan's Article 9 and its non-nuclear stance, and Eisenhower's call for disarmament, point toward giving up nuclear arms, though antimilitarism is not absolute pacifism. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

homestead-ownership.rationale: Antimilitarism is about armies and war, not property theory, and its socialist and liberal strands would split.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Antimilitarism does not address scripture, and its religious and secular strands differ.

equal-conscription.rationale: Liebknecht attacked conscription as the tool of militarism, so antimilitarists would want it ended or, failing that, applied to all. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Antimilitarism is silent on distributive justice; its strands (socialist, libertarian, conservative) split.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Not an antimilitarist question; adherents split by wider politics.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Only the socialist strand holds this; the civil-libertarian and conservative strands do not.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Antimilitarists oppose militarist nationalism but split on patriotism and on working-class politics.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Antimilitarists argue spending should shift from arms to social needs, so cutting welfare to fund arms runs against their priorities. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

former-empire-equal-treatment.rationale: Imperial aspirations are aggressive and opposed. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook. (Carried over from former-empire-influence, "A country should cultivate political and cultural influence in regions once ruled by its predecessor empire.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: Military spending should be cut and the money spent on health, education and development.
missingStatements.rationale: Eisenhower called weapons a theft from the hungry, and the article names diversion of resources from development as a core objection.

missingStatements.text: Standing armies are dangerous to a free people and should be replaced by citizen militias.
missingStatements.rationale: Paris 1899 called standing armies the negation of democratic republics and demanded a citizen army, and Jefferson-style constitutionalists agree.

missingStatements.text: Private arms manufacturers have too much influence over defence and foreign policy.
missingStatements.rationale: Eisenhower warned against the military-industrial complex and the article reports the charge that it pushes for war for private gain.

missingStatements.text: Armed forces should be used only to defend the country against attack, never to start wars.
missingStatements.rationale: Antimilitarism accepts defensive war but opposes aggressive readiness, and Article 9 renounces war as a means of settling disputes.

notes: Strands differ: socialists (Liebknecht) accept citizen militias and class analysis, constitutional conservatives favour citizen militias and non-entanglement, Japanese constitutional pacifism rejects war potential, Thoreau-style libertarians favour civil disobedience. Most non-military statements are inferred and low confidence.
